newsitem.title: CROATIA: EU cancels Mostar bridge ceremony over Croat flag.
newsitem.headline: EU cancels Mostar bridge ceremony over Croat flag.

text.p: The European Union (EU) cancelled a bridge-opening ceremony in the ethnically-divided Bosnian city of Mostar on Friday after a Croatian flag was raised, despite an agreement that national insignia would not be displayed.

The Aviators bridge, which cost 2.1 million marks ($1.37 million), was due to be opened to traffic by the EU's special envoy in Mostar, Sir Martin Garrod, Mayor Ivan Prskalo, a Croat, and EU ambassadors to Bosnia.
"It was agreed and made quite clear to Prskalo that there would be no national flags flying at the bridge," EU spokesman Dragan Gasic told Reuters by telephone.

"The (Croatian) flag was put up there two minutes after the ceremony was due to begin. Then Sir Martin and ambassadors from Austria, France, Sweden, Denmark and Portugal turned around and walked away," Gasic said.
The Bosnian Croat news agency HABENA quoted Prskalo as saying international police removed the flag when he arrived.
"The Croatian flag must not be stripped off Croatian territory, when a mayor, who is a Croat, arrives," HABENA quoted him as saying.
The bridge, financed by the EU, was not opened officially. But people started using it to cross the Neretva river, which divides the town into ethnic Croat and Moslem quarters.

It is one of several bridges across the Neretva River which were destroyed during a vicious war for control of the town between Moslems and Croats in 1993, a side conflict to the main Serb-Moslem struggle.
Mostar's most famous span, known only as "the Old Bridge", was built during Ottoman rule in the 16th century and became a symbol of the town's plight when it was destroyed by the Croats.

After the war Mostar's Moslems and Croats formed a federation under strong pressure from the international community. Their first democratic elections were held last June, supervised by the EU and monitored by NATO peacekeepers, to elect a single city administration.
After alleged irregularities in the voting it took another two months of negotiations to form the city government and elect a Croat mayor and a Moslem deputy.
